literal_meaning: Do something and throw it away

seo.meta_title: 먹어 버렸어 Doesn't Mean 'Throw Away' | Korean -아/어 버리다
seo.meta_description: Word-by-word tools read 버리다 as 'throw away'. After a verb it means 'completely, for good' — with regret, relief or coldness. Here's how to read it.

ai_failure.situation: You see 다 먹어 버렸어 in a webtoon, or 가 버렸어 in a K-pop lyric, and break it down with a dictionary or AI gloss.
ai_failure.ai_mistake: Glosses 버리다 as 'throw away', so 먹어 버렸어 becomes 'ate it and threw it away' and 가 버렸어 'went and threw away'.
ai_failure.why_it_fails: After another verb, 버리다 stops meaning 'throw away'. It says the action is finished completely and can't be undone — and it adds a feeling: regret ('oops'), relief ('finally'), or coldness ('just gone').

natural_solution.rule: Verb + 아/어 버리다 = done completely, for good, with feeling. Read the feeling from the context.

alternatives.context: Regret or cheekiness: 'Oops, I ate the whole cake'
Relief or pride: 'I just got it all done!'
Hurt: 'He just left (and isn't coming back)' — very common in ballads and lyrics
Careful: 'Just give it away (get rid of it)'. Said about a gift, it sounds like you didn't value it.

nuance: Korean often stacks a second verb onto the first to add an attitude instead of a separate action. 버리다 is the most emotional of these helpers. Some combinations have fused into one word: 잊어버리다 ('forget') and 잃어버리다 ('lose') no longer carry much feeling. But in speech, 해 버렸어 still tells the listener how you feel about what happened. A close cousin is -고 말다 (가고 말았다, 'ended up going'), which sounds more written and literary. In everyday speech, 해 버렸어 is the one you'll hear.
